The Crab-plover (Dromas ardeola) exhibits a remarkable life history strategy that begins with the incubation of its large, single, white egg within an underground burrow. The single, large egg weighs 64.83 grams, a substantial investment for a shorebird, reflecting the considerable energy allocated to each offspring. Under controlled laboratory conditions designed to mimic natural nest chamber temperatures, artificial incubation at a constant 36 °C [T = 36 °C] results in a hatchling emerging after precisely 33 days [ab = 33 days]. This incubation period is comparatively long among Charadriiformes, a pattern often linked to the slow embryonic development rates tolerated by the stable, humid microclimate of the subterranean nest. Upon emergence, the precocial chick is remarkably independent, though it still benefits from extensive parental brooding and protection for its initial weeks of life, a period critical for establishing thermoregulatory competence before it begins foraging on its own along the shoreline.

Following emergence, the chick enters a rapid growth phase fueled by both endogenous yolk reserves and protein-rich prey delivered by the adults. At hatching, the wet weight of the neonate is 44 grams [Wwb = 44 grams], a relatively light starting mass given the egg's initial size. However, growth is swift and sustained; under the warm ambient conditions typical of its tropical coastal habitat, where body temperatures routinely reach 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C], the developing chick achieves the capacity for sustained flight and fledging at 49 days after hatching [tx = 49 days after hatching]. This fledging age is intermediate among waders, balancing the need for rapid development to avoid predation with the necessity of attaining sufficient wing and muscle maturity for powered flight. The post-fledging period then involves a gradual transition to independent foraging, with young birds often remaining near their natal burrow for several additional weeks while their hunting proficiency improves.

The species exhibits a rather delayed maturation schedule, a trait that is relatively unusual among small to medium-sized shorebirds. The onset of puberty, defined by the development of functional gonads and associated hormonal changes, is estimated to occur at 147 days after birth [tp = 147 days after birth] when individuals are maintained at an ambient temperature of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]. This relatively early physiological maturation does not, however, translate into immediate breeding. Instead, young Crab-plovers typically defer their first successful reproductive attempt until they have acquired sufficient foraging experience and a suitable nesting territory. Consequently, the first brood is not produced until 365 days since birth [tR = 365 days since birth] under the same thermal regime of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C], highlighting a clear gap between the attainment of sexual maturity and the initiation of actual reproductive effort.

Total lifespan in the Crab-plover is notably extended for a shorebird, with the oldest documented individuals reaching 25 years [am = 25 years] in the wild, a longevity facilitated by their low adult mortality and occupation of relatively predator-safe island nesting sites at a temperature of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]. This extended lifespan allows for repeated reproductive attempts over many seasons, offsetting the species' minimal annual clutch size. The maximum reproductive rate is constrained by the substantial parental investment in a single, large egg. Females typically produce only one egg per clutch [N_R_i = one egg per clutch] and raise a single brood per year [F_R_i = single brood per year], which equates to an annual output of just one egg per year. This remarkably low fecundity is a classic example of a slow life-history strategy, where long adult survival compensates for low per-capita recruitment and the risk of total breeding failure in any given season.

Comparative physiological studies shed further light on the species' metabolic ecology. The ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult Crab-plover is approximately 298 grams [Wwi = approximately 298 grams], placing it among the larger members of its familial sub-group and reflecting the energetic demands of its crab-based diet. This considerable body mass, combined with its specialized diet of crabs and other hard-shelled invertebrates, necessitates a robust digestive and metabolic system. The extended lifespan (25 years) and slow reproductive rate observed in this species are consistent with life-history theory predictions for organisms inhabiting stable, resource-predictable environments. By maximizing adult survival at the expense of annual reproductive output, Dromas ardeola has evolved a successful strategy for thriving on its isolated, predator-limited coastal territories, where competition for high-quality, deep nesting burrows is often the primary constraint on population growth rather than the availability of food for chicks.
